The Agile antechinus (Antechinus agilis) is a small dasyurid marsupial endemic to southeastern Australia, exhibiting a life history strategy characterized by intense, semelparous reproduction. At the body temperatures typical of active thermoregulation in this species, approximately 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], the females undergo a tightly synchronized gestation period lasting 27 days [tg = 27 days]. This brief intrauterine development results in the birth of exceptionally altricial young; each neonate weighs a mere 0.04 grams [Wwb = 0.04 grams] at parturition, a minuscule mass that reflects the energetically constrained resources available during pregnancy for a mammal of this size. The gestation interval is comparable to that of other congeners, though the low birth weight underscores the extreme altriciality typical of the genus. This initial investment is minimal, setting the stage for a prolonged period of dependency within the maternal pouch, during which the neonates will rely entirely on the mother's milk to fuel their rapid growth.

Following their emergence from the pouch, the pups remain suckling and entirely dependent on maternal milk for a sustained period. Under the standard thermoregulatory conditions of approximately 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], the time since birth at weaning extends to 90 days [tx = 90 days]. At this critical developmental milestone, the offspring achieve nutritional independence and transition to a solid diet of invertebrates; their average wet weight at weaning is approximately 10 grams [Wwx = approximately 10 grams]. This represents a substantial increase from the neonatal mass, achieved through a period of rapid growth sustained by the high energetic demands of lactation. The weaning mass of roughly 10 grams [Wwx = roughly 10 grams] is an important benchmark, as the young must attain sufficient body condition to survive their first winter independent of maternal care.

Sexual maturation in the Agile antechinus does not occur immediately after weaning but follows a more prolonged developmental trajectory. At a thermoregulatory set point of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 330 days [tp = 330 days]. Males and females both reach reproductive maturity just prior to the highly synchronous annual breeding period, which typically occurs in late winter. This chronology means that young born in one spring do not become reproductively viable until the following winter, a delay of nearly a full year. The relatively late onset of puberty, for such a short-lived mammal, is a hallmark of the semelparous life history plan, ensuring that all females born in a given cohort are ready to participate in the single, synchronized mating season of their first year of adulthood.

Reproductive output is concentrated into a single, exhaustive breeding season. Females give birth to a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year] at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], with a mean litter size of 10 pups [N_R_i = litter size of 10 pups]. The maximum adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, attained by these females prior to the breeding season averages around 40 grams [Wwi = around 40 grams], which is modest compared to other dasyurids of similar body length, although individuals may range from 16 to 44 grams depending on local resource availability. This body size is modest, yet females must sustain the energetic burden of gestating and suckling a large litter of ten pups. The single annual reproductive event and the substantial investment of producing ten neonates represent an enormous physiological expenditure, which typically results in the death of all males shortly after mating and a high rate of female mortality during lactation.

The lifespan of the Agile antechinus is remarkably short, reflecting its semelparous reproductive strategy. Under the standard thermoregulatory body temperature of approximately 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], the maximum documented longevity is approximately 4.7 years [am = approximately 4.7 years], although most individuals die within their first year of life immediately following the breeding season. The basal metabolic rate, inferred from the closely related brown antechinus (Antechinus stuarti), which strongly resembles this species, is estimated at 36.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 36.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at the same thermal condition at a temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. This elevated metabolic demand, combined with the extreme reproductive effort, drives the catastrophic die-off of males and contributes to the characteristic post-mating mortality. The limited lifespan of approximately four and a half years serves as a maximum boundary, but in practice, ecological mortality far exceeds this upper limit for the vast majority of individuals.
